title: The show starts here: viewers’ interactions with recent television serials’ main title sequences
venue: SoundEffects - An Interdisciplinary Journal of Sound and Sound Experience
finding: Preliminary focus groups (February 2012) with self-identified regular viewers of TV serials: whether a title sequence is watched or skipped depends on a variety of factors; per the author, participants were more likely to keep watching an end-credit sequence whose music changes every episode than an unchanging main title sequence, although for some the titles are required viewing. Qualitative, no group sizes or percentages in the abstract.
why_for_us: An identical intro repeated every episode is the element viewers skip; if we keep a recurring title card, make it very short and vary one audible or visible element per episode.

title: Streaming's Skip Intro Function as a Contradictory Refuge for Television Title Sequences
finding: Essay arguing that the 'skip intro' button, although built to let audiences bypass title sequences, has in practice created a protected space for theme music and title sequences and gives viewers a feeling of agency that matters in post-network, binge-oriented viewing. Argument from industry practice; no viewing data.
why_for_us: Vertical feeds have no skip button, the swipe is the skip: a title card must be short enough that nobody wants to skip it, or sit after the hook so that skipping costs nothing.

title: Immersive Entryways into Televisual Worlds: Affective and Aesthetic Functions of Title Sequences in Quality Series
finding: Essay with three in-depth analyses (Dexter, Six Feet Under, True Blood): immersive title sequences are said to prime viewers' affective appraisal of the show and its leading 'feeling tone', using embodied metaphors and collective imagery that create ambivalent cues and mixed feelings. Close analysis, no audience measurement.
why_for_us: The first seconds should set the feeling tone of the office (warm, slightly ironic, competent) through a concrete tactile image (stamp, paper, keyboard) rather than through a logo.

title: From Saul Bass to participatory culture: Opening title sequences in contemporary television series
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
finding: Essay (cases: Mad Men, The Wire, Game of Thrones, Supernatural): the opening title sequence keeps its paratextual functions (introducing a storyworld, orienting the spectator, managing expectations) and adds a double branding role, branding the content and connecting viewers into 'brand communities'. No audience data.
why_for_us: A recurring title card is a brand asset first and exposition second; design it as a recognisable, shareable signature of 'Komputerku' that the notary community can quote.

title: Reading the Title Sequence ( Vorspann, Générique )
finding: Survey essay on forms and functions of film title sequences; proposes reading the title sequence as self-reflexive, i.e. as a reading of the film in which it is integrated, standing in as 'an alternate kind of movie'. Theoretical, no empirical data.
why_for_us: Treat the title card as a miniature of the series (its joke, its promise) and not as a credits container; in 2-3 seconds it should already say what kind of show this is.

title: Startling or Seductive? An Analysis of Play for Today’s Title Sequences
venue: Journal of British Cinema and Television
finding: Historical analysis of the seven title sequences of the BBC strand Play for Today, based on accounts by producers, composers and graphic designers: two modes of address are identified, 'startling' sequences (1971-3, 1977-82) signalling important, news-adjacent drama, and 'seductive' ones (1973-7) foregrounding humanism and eclecticism. No audience data.
why_for_us: Decide deliberately whether the opening startles or seduces; for a trust-based profession the seductive, humane mode fits the brand, with the startle reserved for the story hook.

title: การออกแบบไตเติ้ลเปิดเรื่องสำหรับภาพยนตร์ชุดทางโทรทัศน์ในยุคหลังปุ่ม “ข้ามบทนำ”
venue: Journal of Fine and Applied Arts Chulalongkorn University
finding: Design analysis of Emmy 'Outstanding Main Title Design' winners 2017-2022 (article in Thai, English abstract): per the author, the skip-intro era opened design possibilities rather than only shortening titles; four elements (visuals, type, audio, time) must work together, and a title sequence serves one of two functions, creating emotion that quickly draws the audience in, or carrying meaning and hints about the story through images and symbols.
why_for_us: Checklist for our title card: picture, lettering, sound and duration designed as one unit, and one clear job (mood or meaning), not both.

title: Don’t Skip Intro. Sigle da non perdere
venue: Nova Science Publishers (Nova Science Publishers, Inc.)
finding: Semiotic essay (in Italian): opening credits evolved from brief, marginal informative texts into refined products designed to present, seduce, involve and ease the viewer's entry into the story; the paper outlines their features, their technology-linked development and the communicative strategies by which they address viewers. No audience data.
why_for_us: Historical support for a short functional opener: the long seductive intro belongs to prestige long-form, while a micro-drama can return to the brief, informative type.

title: títulos de crédito en cine a los opening en series de ficción televisiva: Una evolución histórica desde la perspectiva de las series americanas
finding: Bibliographic review (in Spanish) assembling a chronological line of the origin and evolution of TV series openings ('cabeceras') in the shadow of film title design, intended to explain current design strategies for series openings. Narrative review, no data.
why_for_us: Background source for the history-and-shortening question when we justify a 1-2 second title card.

title: Telenovela: elementos identitários em vinheta de abertura
finding: Historical survey of Rede Globo telenovela openings 1965-2015 analysed with French semiotics (in Portuguese): four recurrently exploited resources are identified, projections of person, time, space, and thematisation procedures, all articulated to produce a sense of identification in the audience. Corpus analysis, no audience measurement.
why_for_us: A telenovela-style opener works by showing who, when, where and what it is about; for us that is the notary, today, the office, the document, compressible into one shot.

title: Intro and Recap Detection for Movies and TV Series
venue: IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
finding: Engineering paper from a streaming service: repetitive intro and recap parts are described as 'unnecessary friction' that customers skip manually, which motivates skip-intro and skip-recap buttons; the authors propose a deep sequence-labelling model (CNN features, B-LSTM, CRF) to detect these segments automatically and report better performance than alternative architectures. No viewer-behaviour numbers in the abstract.
why_for_us: The platform view of repeated intros and recaps is friction to be removed; do not put a repeated block in front of the story in a format where each second is contested.

title: Title Sequences as Paratexts: Narrative Anticipation and Recapitulation
finding: Monograph on the semiotics of title sequences across film history: audiences are said to interpret title sequences as 'paranarrative', engaging them simultaneously as narrative exposition and as production credits; the author states that the theory extends to trailers and commercials. Theory with film examples, no audience data.
why_for_us: A title card can carry exposition (place, profession, tone) at the same moment it names the show, so the two need not cost separate seconds.

title: Divided loyalties: opening sequences in small-screen fantasy adaptations
finding: Essay on teasers ('cold opens') in True Blood, Game of Thrones, Grimm and Once Upon a Time: the teaser must serve as exposition for both the episode and the series while becoming habit-forming, and, in a world of channel-surfing and DVRs, teasers, especially in pilots, must win almost immediate adhesion or lose the potential audience; the cold open is called a crucial structural element for engaging the viewer and establishing the series mythos. Critical analysis, no audience data.
why_for_us: Open every episode cold, with the situation before any title; the pilot's cold open has to explain the series premise and hook at once.

title: Seriality, Repetition and Innovation in Breaking Bad’s Recaps and Teasers
venue: Cinergie – Il Cinema e le altre Arti
finding: Socio-semiotic essay on Breaking Bad: recaps are treated as condensed, functional paratextual thresholds, in contrast to the series' innovative cold opens or teasers, which are designed as textual narrative expansions; a typology of recaps across several seasons is proposed. No audience data.
why_for_us: Keep the two jobs apart: a recap repeats, a cold open adds; in 60-90 s there is room only for the one that adds.

title: Television Spoilers Recast as Narrative Teasers
finding: Online qualitative survey of 43 television time-shifters who knew narrative content before deciding to watch a show: 20 of them cited that content and/or its source as the reason they chose to watch; per the authors, spoilers can function as teasers that lead would-be viewers to enjoyable shows. Small self-selected sample.
why_for_us: Showing a piece of the outcome first (a flash-forward to the awkward moment at the notary's desk) can pull people in rather than spoil the episode.

title: Previously on Supernatural
venue: Revue française des sciences de l’information et de la communication
finding: Essay (in French): the 'previously on' segment of Supernatural is analysed as a space both external and internal to the fiction where the series designates its identity, comments on and even rewrites itself, and addresses fans directly by anticipating their reception. No audience data.
why_for_us: If we ever use a recap, treat it as a voice of the series (a wink at regular viewers) and not as a plot summary.

title: Previously On: Prime Time Serials and the Mechanics of Memory
finding: Book chapter (in the volume Intermediality and Storytelling) on prime-time serials and memory; no abstract in OpenAlex, so no finding is reported here.
why_for_us: Pointer for the question of how serials help viewers remember earlier episodes; read before deciding on any recap device.

title: Musical Soundtracks as a Schematic Influence on the Cognitive Processing of Filmed Events
finding: Experiment with three ambiguous film clips shown with positive, negative or no music: per the author, relative to no music, positive and negative music significantly biased viewers' interpretation (predicted ending, character personality and motives) and their recognition memory a week later in a mood-congruent direction. No effect sizes in the abstract.
why_for_us: The first notes decide how an ambiguous first shot is read; choose opening music by the interpretation we want of the client or notary on screen.

title: When Your Ear Sets the Stage: Musical Context Effects in Film Perception
finding: Covert-design experiment (N = 48): participants saw a visually identical film sequence with either the original or a 'fake' score and then wrote plot continuations; content analysis showed that anticipations about the further development were systematically influenced by the music, per the author.
why_for_us: Music at the start sets what viewers expect to happen next; a jingle in the wrong mood creates the wrong expectation for the following 60 seconds.

title: Film music influences how viewers relate to movie characters.
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics Creativity and the Arts
finding: Experiment with clips of characters' neutral or ambiguous reactions under thriller music, melodrama music or no music: both music conditions differed significantly from no music; compared with melodramatic music, thriller music significantly lowered character likability and certainty about the character's thoughts, per the authors.
why_for_us: Tense, thriller-like opening music would make the notary less likable; a warm motif under the first appearance of the protagonist supports liking.

title: How Soundtracks Shape What We See: Analyzing the Influence of Music on Visual Scenes Through Self-Assessment, Eye Tracking, and Pupillometry
finding: Two between-subjects studies (online N = 118; lab replication N = 92 with eye tracking and pupillometry) on an unknown movie scene scored with melancholic vs anxious music: the score changed empathy toward the character, impressions of his personality, plot anticipations and perception of the environment (melancholic: more empathy, cozier setting); the anxious score widened pupils and increased time spent looking at a hard-to-notice background character, per the authors.
why_for_us: Same shot, different music, different office: a calm motif makes the room feel cozy, an anxious one makes viewers scan for details and threats; pick per episode goal.

title: On music’s potential to convey meaning in film: A systematic review of empirical evidence
finding: Systematic review of 24 German- and English-language empirical studies: differently connoted music or music of different genres triggers supra-individual associations that make recipients' perceptions and evaluations of plot and protagonists predictable, depending on the realism and abstraction level of the audio-visual stimulus, per the author.
why_for_us: A motif's genre connotation is read in a similar way by most viewers, so a consistent sonic identity can cue genre (light office comedy) reliably.

title: Zur Bedeutungsvermittlung von Filmmusik
finding: Experiment (69 students, in German) on the opening music of Hitchcock's Spellbound: listeners who took it in unconsciously as background reported only a vague, diffuse quality ('drama'), while those who attended to the changing motifs perceived graded bipolar structures matching the composer's intention, also among those unfamiliar with the film. Chapter in an edited volume; English abstract is a machine translation per the record.
why_for_us: Most viewers will hear the opening music as background and take away one diffuse quality; give a jingle one unmistakable mood and do not expect it to carry two messages.

title: Recognizing and Naming Tunes: Memory Impairment in the Elderly
finding: Recognition study with adults over 50 using theme tunes of remote, recent and frequent TV programmes: for programmes participants had watched, older subjects recognised fewer tunes as familiar and were less able to name the programme; neither amount of exposure nor delay since exposure significantly influenced these age-related impairments, per the author. A study of ageing and memory, not of marketing.
why_for_us: Theme tunes are recognised as familiar more easily than they are linked to the programme name; pair the jingle with the spoken or written title each time.

title: A música nas aberturas das telenovelas da Rede Globo de Televisão no período de 1970 a 2012: funções e dramaturgia musical
finding: Analysis of 248 telenovela openings ('vinhetas') aired by Rede Globo 1970-2012 (in Portuguese): openings fall into four groups, portraying the main character, the place, the era, or an important aspect of the story; music is either a song or instrumental and either complements the images or is solely responsible for revealing the context and dramatic focus, per the authors. Descriptive corpus analysis, no audience data.
why_for_us: In the telenovela tradition the opening music may alone tell where and what the story is; a 2-second motif with a 'kancelaria' colour (typewriter, stamp, piano) can do the scene-setting.

title: Sound Bridging the Apocalypse: Sonically Integrating the Title Sequence as Audiovisual Paratext in THE WALKING DEAD (2010–2022)
finding: Analysis of every episode of The Walking Dead: four ways of sonically joining cold open and title sequence are identified (no preparation, rhythmic or textural build-up, cue transition, sound bridge); per the author, even when the titles are skipped a tension-and-release dynamic is preserved, the momentum of the cold-open cliffhanger resolving in the final note of the title sequence. No audience data.
why_for_us: Let the hook's last sound run into the title card (sound bridge) and let the jingle's final note be the release; the title then reads as part of the scene.

title: テレビドラマ「おしん」のテーマ音楽聴取に関する定性的研究
venue: 尚美学園大学芸術情報学部紀要
finding: Qualitative study by the composer of the NHK drama Oshin (in Japanese): 10 music students individually listened to the theme music while watching the title background footage and were interviewed (semi-structured, free association) about the images of the drama's content they formed; the author reports individual differences in how the theme music's functions were received and draws no universal rules. University bulletin, n = 10, author studies his own work.
why_for_us: Even a famous theme produces differing images across listeners; test our jingle on a handful of notaries before fixing it.

title: SOUND ACROSS SERIES Theme tunes as leitmotif in Chris Lilley's television series
venue: Screen Sound Journal (per landing page; OpenAlex lists no venue)
finding: Essay on the comedian-composer Chris Lilley's five series: the authors argue that his use of sound, particularly original music, brands individual series and creates a cross-series form of sonic identification. No audience data.
why_for_us: A small recurring motif can tie separate episodes (and later spin-offs or ads) to one maker; keep the same motif across all 'Komputerku' material.

title: The TV series pilot: analysis of «Aída», the first spanish spin off
finding: Essay with a case analysis (Spanish sitcom Aída): the author works from the stated principle that in the Spanish TV market no new programme stays on air if after four episodes its share is below the channel average, so the pilot must secure audience involvement and identification; the pilot must present what makes the series different: concept, tone, narrative structure, sets and character design. The four-episode rule is the author's premise, not a tested result.
why_for_us: The pilot has to show concept, tone, structure, setting and characters in full; plan on a window of about four episodes to prove the series.

title: Pilot, l’importanza della prima impressione
finding: Essay (in Italian) on the pilot as first impression: in a single episode the pilot can show only the surface of a series and must convince the network before the audience; the bond between audience and series is compared to an affective relationship in which the first impression is fundamental, and the author asks whether binge-watching and on-demand platforms minimise the impact of this special episode. Questions and argument, no data.
why_for_us: The pilot's task is to make viewers like the people and the atmosphere of the office, more than to explain the product.

title: Predicting New TV Series Ratings from their Pilot Episode Scripts
finding: Model tested on 116 hour-long scripted series that debuted on the four major US networks in 2009-2014: per the authors, the size of the main component of the text network built from the pilot script 'strongly explains' the number of viewers of the first several episodes. Correlational; published in a journal of doubtful standing (CCSE).
why_for_us: Weak hint that a pilot built around a connected set of concepts draws more early viewers; treat as a hypothesis only.

title: Binge Watching and Advertising
finding: Model of Hulu viewing data decomposing behaviour into whether the user continues the session after each episode, whether the next episode is from the same series, and the time between sessions; drivers are split into user traits and states created by previously viewed content, and advertising responsiveness differs between bingers and non-bingers and changes within a session, per the authors. No coefficients in the abstract.
why_for_us: Continuation is decided after every episode, and what was just watched changes the odds; each episode opening is also the continuation prompt for someone arriving from the previous one.

title: Going Viral, Binge-Watching, and Attention Cannibalism
finding: Statistical modelling of one season of a streaming original: onset of viewing is modelled with a change point between 'epidemic' and 'endemic' phases, and time to complete the season with a negative binomial hurdle model that separates binge racers (all episodes in one day) from other viewers; used to study 'attention cannibalism' between simultaneously released programmes. Methods paper, no retention percentages in the abstract.
why_for_us: Viewers split into those who take the whole season in one sitting and the rest; release all episodes so that the pilot can lead straight into episode 2.

title: Accelerating the flow: A transition effect in programming theory?
finding: Analysis of 240 transitions between prime-time programmes on the four US broadcast networks: a modest transition effect was found, associated with new fall schedules but not familiar spring schedules; programme endings had a significant impact on duplicated viewers in the subsequent programme, while approaches to programme starts had become standardised in the early 1990s, per the authors.
why_for_us: Carry-over into the next item depended on how the previous one ended; in an autoplay feed, the end of episode N is part of the opening of episode N+1.

title: May the Giant Be With You: Twin Peaks Season Two, Episode One and the Television Auteur
venue: UEL Research Repository (University of East London)
finding: Essay: the season-two premiere of Twin Peaks drew some of the series' highest ratings, yet, per the author, its slow-paced opening scenes and deliberately confusing material flouted television conventions and 'in response the following week the ratings dropped dramatically'. A single case; the causal link is the author's interpretation, and no figures are given in the abstract.
why_for_us: A premiere that opens slowly and confuses can cost the next episode's audience; keep the pilot opening clear and brisk.

title: Establishing Shot Type Affects Arousal and Cognitive Load During Transitions Between Novel Interior Locations in Films
finding: Lab experiment (pupil diameter by eye tracking, prefrontal oxygenation by fNIRS) comparing four establishing-shot types and none before scenes in new interior locations: geographic establishing shots produced significantly lower average pupil diameter than all other types and no establishing shot, and establishing shots showing the actors gave lower pupil diameter than none (alpha 0.05); fNIRS results diverged from pupil results, per the authors. Sample size not in the abstract.
why_for_us: One wide shot that places the notary in the office lowers the load of entering the scene; it can be very short but should not be dropped.

title: Recognizing the setting before reporting the action: investigating how visual events are mentally constructed from scene images
finding: Doctoral dissertation with masking and eye-movement experiments on scene images: scene categorisation reached ceiling within a single fixation, whereas basic-level action categorisation needed two to three fixations and was not at ceiling at a 367 ms SOA; the author concludes that the scene category is the first construct used to represent an event, possibly also in film openings.
why_for_us: Viewers know where they are within one glance and need longer to see what is being done; make the setting instantly legible and hold the first action for about a second.

title: Manipulating Montage: Effects on Film Comprehension, Recall, Person Perception, and Aesthetic Responses
finding: Experiment with a short narrative film edited four ways, varying deviation from linear order: recall of action and reconstruction of event order were strongly associated with montage linearity; negative information presented at the end led to more negative impressions of the protagonist, and spectators increasingly disliked the less 'filmic' versions even when they could reconstruct the order, per the author. One relatively deviant version gave the most accurate perception of the protagonists.
why_for_us: Non-linear openings cost recall and can cost liking; if we open with a flash-forward, keep the rest strictly linear.

title: The establishment of interpretative expectations in film
finding: Small exploratory study with a discourse-linguistic framework: film beginnings show differing organisational features that correlate with the narrative strategy of the film as a whole, so beginnings act as indicators of the film's 'method of development' and set up expectations that guide hypotheses and selective attention, per the authors.
why_for_us: The way the first seconds are organised teaches viewers how to watch the rest; keep the same opening grammar in every episode so the format becomes learnable.

title: Narrative versus style: Effect of genre-typical events versus genre-typical filmic realizations on film viewers’ genre recognition
finding: Journal article on film viewers' genre recognition from genre-typical events versus genre-typical filmic realisation; no abstract in OpenAlex, so no finding is reported here.
why_for_us: Pointer for the question of whether style or events tell viewers the genre in the opening; read before deciding how to signal 'comedy' in the first shot.

title: In the beginning
finding: Essay on how documentary films begin: beginnings launch a narrative trajectory by altering the sense of time and stress different qualities, from identifying a problem (a 'lack' that calls for a response) to establishing a mood; the author notes that beginnings have received little scrutiny. No audience data.
why_for_us: Two legitimate jobs for an opening: state the lack (a deed that cannot be signed, a missing document) or set the mood; pick one per episode.

title: Cinematic Overtures: How to Read Opening Scenes
finding: Book of close readings of opening sequences by leading directors, on the premise that a film's first few minutes provide the key to the rest of the film. Criticism, no audience data.
why_for_us: Source of worked examples of opening scenes for the writers' room.

title: Att höra genre : Vad i ljudet i filmens inledning berättar om genre
venue: DiVA (student thesis; OpenAlex lists no venue)
finding: Student thesis (in Swedish) analysing the sound of the first five minutes of six films from different genres: opening sound can indicate genre, most clearly in adventure and action, less clearly in comedy, and in some films the opening sound instead describes place or ethnicity, per the author. Six films, no listeners tested.
why_for_us: Comedy is the genre least clearly announced by sound alone; signal it through the picture and the first line as well as the jingle.

title: Designing for Curiosity: Discovering and Testing Communicative Structures That Elicit Curiosity
finding: Three studies using narrative openings as a model system: an inductive analysis of bestselling fiction identified five recurring 'curiosity scaffolding' structures; passages built with them elicited greater curiosity than closely matched controls (Study 2), and readers preferentially selected such passages (Study 3), per the authors. Preprint; the five structures and effect sizes are not named in the abstract.
why_for_us: Closest experimental support for writing the first line as a deliberate curiosity structure; read the full text for the five structures before drafting episode openers.

title: Large‐scale log analysis of digital reading
venue: Proceedings of the Association for Information Science and Technology
finding: Analysis of 10 months of reading logs from the commercial e-book service Bookmate (Russia): parallel reading and book abandonment 'occur very frequently'; genre affects some reading behaviours, while gender and book length appear to matter less, per the authors. No abandonment percentages in the abstract.
why_for_us: Abandonment is the normal case in digital consumption; assume most starters will not finish a season and put the product message early.

title: Penser le commencement : la première phrase de roman passée au filtre cognitif de la causalité
finding: Conference paper (in French): the first sentence of a novel presents an event with no known cause, which troubles a cognition that relies on causal continuity; the author hypothesises that readers develop compensatory strategies and reports first results of a sketch of an experiment with English-speaking subjects. Results are not given in the abstract.
why_for_us: An opening line creates a causal gap the audience wants to close; start on an effect whose cause is withheld for a few seconds.

title: Thresholds and What Seems to Be: Munro’s First Sentences
venue: ELOPE English Language Overseas Perspectives and Enquiries
finding: Overview of the first sentences of Alice Munro's 149 stories in 14 collections: great stylistic variety (short declaratives, multi-line sentences, many foregrounding past time), with one constant per the authors, a tension between what is realistic and tangible and what lies beneath or hidden. Literary analysis, no reader data.
why_for_us: A mundane, concrete first line that hints at something hidden suits an office setting: an ordinary sentence at the desk with one detail that is off.

title: Openings: Narrative Beginnings from the Epic to the Novel
venue: Oxford University Press (per DOI; OpenAlex lists no venue)
finding: Monograph from Greek and Roman epic to the modern novel: Homer set a rule by plunging in medias res, and later writers persistently play this 'interventionist' opening against a sense of a 'deep', natural beginning (Genesis, a birth). Literary history, no reader data.
why_for_us: In medias res is the oldest opening convention; begin in the middle of the appointment, not with the client arriving.

title: Strategie di scrittura e atti di lettura nella prima frase delle Novelle per un anno
venue: Archive of Doctoral Theses and Digital Collections (University of Calabria)
finding: Essay (in Italian) on the first sentences of Pirandello's Novelle per un anno: a refined in medias res technique is used to prompt, implicitly or explicitly, the reader's questions about the characters and events about to be staged; the essay examines sentence arrangement and the relation to the title. Literary analysis, no reader data.
why_for_us: Write the first line so that it makes the viewer ask who this is and what has just happened, and let the episode title sharpen that question.

title: The impact of tutorials on games of varying complexity
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Multivariate field study with over 45,000 players, eight tutorial designs in three games: tutorials increased play time by as much as 29% in the most complex game but did not significantly improve engagement in the two simpler games; per the authors, investment in tutorials may not be justified where mechanics can be discovered through experimentation.
why_for_us: Explanatory openers pay off only when the content is complex; a simple office comedy needs no set-up preamble, while an episode about a difficult procedure may.

title: Show or Tell? A Comparison of Direct Instruction Tutorial and Learn By Doing Increased Impasse Versions of Initial Levels of a Puzzle Game
venue: International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games (FDG)
finding: Experiment with 75 players (up to 20 minutes) on three versions of the first seven levels of Baba Is You: players of the tutorialised version made fewer mistakes and rated difficulty lower, while all groups scored highly on content knowledge and engagement; per the authors, direct instruction at the start gives equal understanding more quickly without sacrificing engagement.
why_for_us: A brief explicit orientation at the start (one line saying who and where) need not reduce engagement.

title: Demystifying the First-Time Experience of Mobile Games: The Presence of a Tutorial Has a Positive Impact on Non-Expert Players’ Flow and Continuous-Use Intentions
finding: Laboratory experiment with 40 players: in a simple game, a tutorial had a positive impact on non-expert players' perceived flow and no effect on experts' flow; flow had a positive impact on continuous-use intentions for both groups, per the authors, who note that many mobile players abandon a game within 24 h of download.
why_for_us: Orientation helps newcomers and does not harm insiders: the pilot can explain the office for non-notaries without boring notaries, if it is short.

title: Evaluating the Onboarding Phase of Free-toPlay Mobile Games: A Mixed-Method Approach
venue: Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play
finding: Lab mixed-methods study (28 participants, three free-to-play mobile titles; heart-rate variability, skin conductance, stimulated recall, engagement graphs, flow and post-game questionnaires) of the first few minutes of play, a phase the authors say typically shows substantial churn; it evaluates the research techniques and gives an empirically based recommendation of design elements that produce high arousal (elements not named in the abstract).
why_for_us: A method template for testing our first seconds: second-by-second engagement graphs plus recall interviews with a small panel of notaries.

title: The effectiveness of movie trailer advertising
finding: Event study and cross-sectional analysis on a sample of movie trailers: the appeal of the plot revealed in the trailer, the number of scene cuts and the inclusion of violent, sexual or humorous scenes influence the movie's abnormal stock returns, while special effects do not; investors react more strongly to first than to follow-up trailers, and early release of the first trailer has a positive effect, per the authors. The outcome is investor reaction, not audience behaviour.
why_for_us: For a series teaser: reveal an appealing plot, cut briskly and include humour; the first teaser carries most of the weight.

title: Do EEG Metrics Derived from Trailers Predict the Commercial Success of Movies? A Systematic Analysis of Five Independent Datasets
finding: Systematic analysis of EEG from 188 participants viewing 161 movie trailers across five datasets: of the metrics tested (alpha, theta, beta, gamma, alpha asymmetry, intersubject correlation) only gamma activity predicted box office beyond movie characteristics and self-reported liking, including out of sample; the authors give initial evidence that the gamma response reflects understanding and comprehension.
why_for_us: What predicts success in a teaser is whether people understand it; make the premise of 'Komputerku' graspable in the opening instead of mysterious.

title: The Role of Music in Motion Picture Advertising and Theatrical Trailers: Altering Music to Modify Emotional Response and Genre Expectations
finding: Study of whether emotions evoked by the music of a theatrical trailer relate to viewers' expectations of the film's genre; the OpenAlex record holds only the introduction and literature review, so results are not available here. Published in a journal of doubtful standing.
why_for_us: Pointer only: music as a genre cue in trailers; do not cite for results.

title: Opening big in box office? Trailer content can help
venue: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics Speech and Signal Processing
finding: Regression analysis on a database of 474 American movie trailers: features capturing the emotional information in the audiovisual stream had as much predictive information for opening-weekend financial success as metadata features and improved prediction when added, per the authors. Predictive, not causal.
why_for_us: The emotional signal of a short audiovisual teaser carries measurable information about uptake; track the emotional profile of our teaser cuts.
